lessons.title: in / out Variance (Declaration-Site Variance)
lessons.content: Kotlin lets you declare variance at the class definition instead of at every use site (unlike Java's wildcards). `out T` means the type is only ever produced/returned (covariant) - so List<Dog> can be used where List<Animal> is expected. `in T` means the type is only ever consumed/accepted (contravariant) - so Comparator<Animal> can be used where Comparator<Dog> is expected. Real scenario: designing a Repository<out T> interface so a Repository<PremiumUser> can be passed anywhere a Repository<User> is expected, without unsafe casts.

lessons.title: Star Projections & Use-Site Variance
lessons.content: When you don't know or care about the exact type parameter, use `*` (star projection) - e.g. List<*> means 'a list of something, I only care that it's a List'. Use-site variance (`Array<out Any>` as a function parameter) is for when the class itself isn't declared variant, but you only need read or write access in that specific spot. Real scenario: a logging function that accepts any Repository<*> just to log its class name, without needing to know T.

lessons.title: Reified Type Parameters
lessons.content: Generics are erased at runtime in Kotlin/JVM - normally you can't do `T::class` inside a generic function. `inline fun <reified T>` keeps the type information available at the call site by inlining the function body, letting you do type checks and reflection that would otherwise require passing a Class<T> parameter manually. Real scenario: a type-safe Intent extras reader or a JSON deserializer helper that infers the target type from the call site instead of an explicit Class parameter.

codeSnippets.code:
inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T =
    this.fromJson(json, T::class.java)

// call site - no Class<T> argument needed:
val user: User = gson.fromJson(jsonString)
